question.explanation:
We recognize that the series looks similar to the Maclaurin expansion for $f(x) = e^x.$

\begin{align*} e^x =1 + x + \dfrac{x^2}{2!} + \dfrac{x^3}{3!} + \cdots + \dfrac{x^n}{n!}+ \cdots \end{align*}

Substituting $x={\color{blue}1}$ into our Maclaurin expansion gives

\begin{align*} e^1 &=1 + {\color{blue}1}+ \dfrac{{\color{blue}1}^2}{2!} + \dfrac{{\color{blue}1}^3}{3!} + \cdots + \dfrac{{\color{blue}1}^n}{n!}+ \cdots\\[5pt] e &=2 + \dfrac{1}{2!} + \dfrac{1}{3!} + \cdots + \dfrac{1}{n!}+ \cdots\, . \end{align*}

Therefore, the sum of the series is $e.$

Then, we recognize that the series looks similar to the Maclaurin expansion for $f(x) = e^x.$

\begin{align*} e^x =1 + {\color{blue}x} + \dfrac{{\color{blue}x}^2}{2!} + \dfrac{{\color{blue}x}^3}{3!} + \cdots +\dfrac{{\color{blue}x}^n}{n!} + \cdots \end{align*}

Substituting $x={\color{blue}-3}$ into our Maclaurin expansion gives

\begin{align*} e^{-3 } &=1 + ({\color{blue}-3}) + \dfrac{({\color{blue}-3})^2}{2!} + \dfrac{({\color{blue}-3})^3}{3!}+\dfrac{({\color{blue}-3})^4}{4!} + \cdots +\dfrac{({\color{blue}-3})^n}{n!} + \cdots\\[5pt] e^{-3 } & = 1-3 +\dfrac{9}{2} - \dfrac{27}{3\cdot 2}+ \dfrac{81}{4!} -\dfrac{243}{5!}+ \cdots + \dfrac{(-3)^{n}}{n!}+\cdots\\[5pt] & = -2+ \dfrac{81}{4!} -\dfrac{243}{5!}+ \cdots + \dfrac{(-3)^{n}}{n!}+\cdots\, . \end{align*}

Therefore, the sum of the series is $e^{-3}.$

question.explanation:
Notice that we can rewrite the given sum as follows: \begin{align} \sqrt{3} - 1 - \dfrac{(\sqrt{3} - 1)^2}{2} + \dfrac{(\sqrt{3} - 1)^3}{3} - \cdots + \dfrac{(-1)^{n+1}(\sqrt{3} - 1)^n}{n} + \cdots & = \\[5pt] ({\color{blue}\sqrt{3} - 1}) - \dfrac{({\color{blue}\sqrt{3} - 1})^2}{2}+ \dfrac{({\color{blue}\sqrt{3} - 1})^3}{3} - \cdots + \dfrac{(-1)^{n+1}({\color{blue}\sqrt{3} - 1})^n}{n}+\cdots & \end{align}

Then, we recognize that the series looks similar to the Maclaurin expansion for $f(x) = \ln(1+x).$ \begin{align*} \ln(1+x) = {\color{blue}x} - \frac{{\color{blue}x}^2}{2} + \frac{{\color{blue}x}^3}{3} - \cdots + \dfrac{(-1)^{n+1}({\color{blue}x})^n}{n} + \cdots \end{align*}

Substituting $x = {\color{blue}\sqrt{3} - 1}$ into our Maclaurin expansion gives \begin{align*} \ln(1 + {\color{blue}\sqrt{3} - 1}) & = ({\color{blue}\sqrt{3}-1}) - \frac{({\color{blue}\sqrt{3}-1})^2}{2} + \frac{({\color{blue}\sqrt{3} - 1})^3}{3} - \cdots + \dfrac{(-1)^{n+1}({\color{blue}\sqrt{3} - 1})^n}{n} + \cdots\\[5pt] \ln(\sqrt{3}) & = \sqrt{3} - 1 - \dfrac{(\sqrt{3}-1)^2}{2} + \dfrac{(\sqrt{3} - 1)^3}{3} - \cdots + \dfrac{(-1)^{n+1}(\sqrt{3} - 1)^n}{n} + \cdots\\[5pt] \dfrac{1}{2} \ln{3} & = \sqrt{3} - 1 - \dfrac{(\sqrt{3} - 1)^2}{2} + \dfrac{(\sqrt{3} - 1)^3}{3} - \cdots + \dfrac{(-1)^{n+1}(\sqrt{3} - 1)^n}{n} + \cdots. \end{align*}

Therefore, the sum of the series is $\dfrac{1}{2}\ln{3}.$

question.text: Find the sum of the following series. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
We recognize that the series looks similar to the Maclaurin expansion for $f(x) = e^x.$

$$ \begin{align*} e^x = 1 + x + \dfrac{x^2}{2!} + \dfrac{x^3}{3!} + \cdots + \dfrac{x^n}{n!} + \cdots \end{align*} $$

Substituting $x = {\color{blue}-\sqrt{7}}$ into our Maclaurin expansion gives

$$ \begin{align*} e^{-\sqrt{7}} &= 1 + \left({\color{blue}-\sqrt{7}}\right) + \dfrac{\left({\color{blue}-\sqrt{7}}\right)^2}{2!} + \dfrac{\left({\color{blue}-\sqrt{7}}\right)^3}{3!} + \cdots + \dfrac{\left({\color{blue}-\sqrt{7}}\right)^n}{n!} + \cdots \\[5pt] e^{-\sqrt{7}} &= 1 - \sqrt{7} + \dfrac{7}{2!} - \dfrac{7\sqrt{7}}{3!} + \cdots + \dfrac{(-\sqrt{7})^n}{n!} + \cdots . \end{align*} $$

Therefore, the sum of the series is $\bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{e^{-\sqrt{7}}}.$

question.text:
Find the sum $S$ of the series

$$ S = \left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - 1\right) - \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - 1\right)^2}{2} + \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - 1\right)^3}{3} - \cdots + \dfrac{(-1)^{n+1}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - 1\right)^n}{n} + \cdots $$

Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
Notice that we can rewrite the given sum as follows: \begin{align} \left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - 1\right) - \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - 1\right)^2}{2} + \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - 1\right)^3}{3} - \cdots + \dfrac{(-1)^{n+1}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - 1\right)^n}{n} + \cdots & = \\[5pt] \left({\color{blue}\dfrac{\pi}{4} - 1}\right) - \dfrac{\left({\color{blue}\dfrac{\pi}{4} - 1}\right)^2}{2} + \dfrac{\left({\color{blue}\dfrac{\pi}{4} - 1}\right)^3}{3} - \cdots + \dfrac{(-1)^{n+1}\left({\color{blue}\dfrac{\pi}{4} - 1}\right)^n}{n} + \cdots & \end{align}

Then, we recognize that the series looks similar to the Maclaurin expansion for $f(x) = \ln(1+x).$ \begin{align*} \ln(1+x) = {\color{blue}x} - \frac{{\color{blue}x}^2}{2}+\frac{{\color{blue}x}^3}{3} - \cdots + \dfrac{(-1)^{n+1}{\color{blue}x}^n}{n} + \cdots \end{align*}

Substituting $x = {\color{blue}\dfrac{\pi}{4} - 1}$ into our Maclaurin expansion gives \begin{align*} \ln\left(1 + {\color{blue}\dfrac{\pi}{4} - 1}\right) & = \left({\color{blue}\dfrac{\pi}{4} - 1}\right) - \dfrac{\left({\color{blue}\dfrac{\pi}{4} - 1}\right)^2}{2} + \dfrac{\left({\color{blue}\dfrac{\pi}{4} - 1}\right)^3}{3} - \cdots + \dfrac{(-1)^{n+1}\left({\color{blue}\dfrac{\pi}{4} - 1}\right)^n}{n} + \cdots\\[5pt] \ln\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) & = \left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - 1\right) - \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - 1\right)^2}{2} + \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - 1\right)^3}{3} - \cdots + \dfrac{(-1)^{n+1}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - 1\right)^n}{n} + \cdots. \end{align*}

Therefore, the sum of the series is $\bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{\ln\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)}.$
